name: Bimatoprost

lead: Bimatoprost is a prostaglandin analogue approved as Latisse for eyelash hypotrichosis. It gives longer, thicker, darker lashes, which frames the eyes and makes the eye area look more defined. Some people also use it on eyebrows.

It is thought to prolong the growth phase of lash follicles, increase the number of follicles growing at once, and darken lashes through pigment production. Randomised trials report increases in lash length, thickness and darkness over vehicle. It was first approved as eye drops for glaucoma and received its lash approval in 2008 after patients noticed longer, darker lashes.

paras: It is applied along the upper lash line as a prescription solution, usually as a nightly routine, with careful application at the lash line. Lash changes build over weeks of regular use, and lashes return to baseline after people stop. Eyebrow use is off-label and based on small studies and user reports.

Common effects are eye redness, itching and darkening of the eyelid skin. It can cause permanent darkening of the iris, particularly in hazel or mixed-colour eyes, and periorbital fat loss that gives a sunken look. It is prescription-only in the United States; over-the-counter lash serums are regulated as cosmetics, not drugs.

angle.text: Bimatoprost is used to get longer, fuller, darker lashes, sometimes on brows too, for a more defined eye area. It prolongs the lash growth phase so more and longer lashes grow in. Lash growth is well studied; iris colour change and periorbital fat loss are known side effects.

lead: Bimatoprost is a synthetic prostamide, a structural analogue of prostaglandin F2-alpha, applied to the eye or eyelid margin. It is sold as Lumigan and generics for open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension, and as Latisse for eyelash hypotrichosis [1][2]. The US Food and Drug Administration approved it for glaucoma in 2001 [1].

In appearance communities it is used to lengthen, thicken and darken eyelashes, and some users apply it to eyebrows off-label. Randomised trials of the 0.03% solution reported increases in lash length, fullness and darkness over vehicle, and the effect is described as fading after use stops [2][3][4]. Small studies have also examined eyebrow and scalp use, but these are not approved indications [5][6].

Documented adverse effects include conjunctival redness, itching, darkening of the eyelid skin, and permanent iris darkening; periorbital fat changes have also been reported [7][1][2]. The drug is prescription-only in the United States, and over-the-counter lash serums are regulated as cosmetics rather than drugs [2][8].
infobox: Ophthalmic drops; eyelid-margin application (cosmetic); intracameral implant (glaucoma)

paras: Bimatoprost is used in adults with open-angle glaucoma or ocular hypertension, alone or combined with the beta blocker timolol [1][7]. The US label describes it as a prostaglandin analogue indicated to reduce elevated intraocular pressure [9]. Network meta-analyses and head-to-head trials have compared it with timolol, latanoprost and travoprost; Wikipedia summarises these as finding it more effective than timolol and at least as effective as latanoprost and travoprost at lowering pressure [1][10][11][12][13].
A sustained-release intracameral implant has also been approved for glaucoma, with effects lasting about a year, as described in a 2025 review of new glaucoma treatments [14].

The 0.03% solution is approved as Latisse for eyelash hypotrichosis, a condition of inadequate or sparse lashes. Wikipedia notes the approval is for essentially cosmetic purposes [1]. According to Grokipedia, the approval followed observations of lash growth in glaucoma patients, and the label regimen is a nightly application to the upper eyelid margin with a sterile single-use applicator [2].

Off-label uses described in the literature include eyebrow hypotrichosis and scalp hair loss. A 2011 placebo-controlled study of the drug on eyebrows was registered on ClinicalTrials.gov [5], and a pilot randomised trial compared it with mometasone in scalp alopecia areata [6].

In the phase III trials summarised by Grokipedia, nightly application for 16 weeks increased lash length by about 25 percent, fullness by about 106 percent and darkness by about 18 percent versus vehicle, with visible change typically from about four weeks and full effect at 12 to 16 weeks [2]. Published reviews of bimatoprost for lash hypotrichosis describe the trial programme and adverse-event rates [15][16]. A 2024 review of eyelash serums concluded that the prostaglandin analogues have the stronger evidence base among lash products, while non-prostaglandin serums vary [8].

Eyebrows: a small placebo-controlled study of Latisse for eyebrow hypotrichosis (n=20) was completed in 2011 [5]. A published case report described increased eyebrow hair growth and thickening in a woman after eight months of daily use [1].

Scalp: a pilot randomised study compared bimatoprost with mometasone furoate in scalp alopecia areata [6]. A phase 1 safety and pharmacokinetic study in men with androgenetic alopecia was registered and terminated [17]. Reviews of chemotherapy-induced alopecia list other interventions and do not establish bimatoprost as an approved option [18].

Glaucoma: large randomised trials have compared bimatoprost with timolol, latanoprost and travoprost over 12 weeks to 12 months [10][11][12][13][19]. A network meta-analysis of 114 randomised trials ranked first-line glaucoma medications by pressure reduction [20], and an earlier meta-analysis covered the main drug classes [21].

The most common effect is conjunctival hyperemia (redness), reported in more than 10 percent of patients on the eye-drop formulation, and the US label cites 45 percent for the most common reaction [1][9]. Other reported effects include itching, burning, blurred vision, and eyelash changes [1][9].

The label warns of pigmentation of the iris, periorbital tissue (eyelid) and eyelashes. Iris pigmentation is likely to be permanent, while lash changes are usually reversible [9]. Wikipedia reports that cosmetic-formulation effects include eyelid or under-eye darkening and infection if single-use applicators are reused [1]. Grokipedia additionally lists periorbital fat atrophy and unintended hair growth where the solution contacts skin [2]. Wikipedia reports a study suggesting that blotting excess solution after drop instillation was associated with shorter lashes and less eyelid pigmentation [1].

The label also lists intraocular inflammation, macular edema and hypersensitivity as warnings or contraindications [9]. Regarding pregnancy, the label states there are no adequate controlled studies in pregnant women, and that high oral doses caused abortion and early delivery in mice and rats [9]. Wikipedia states use in pregnancy and breastfeeding is generally not recommended [1].

For intraocular pressure, bimatoprost is believed to raise aqueous humour outflow through the trabecular meshwork and uveoscleral routes [9]. Wikipedia notes that, unlike other prostaglandin analogues, it does not act on the prostaglandin F receptor and is thought to mimic prostamides, for which no receptor had been identified as of 2015 [1]. Reviews of the pharmacology are available [22][23].

For lashes, the proposed explanation is that it prolongs the anagen growth phase and increases the proportion of follicles in that phase, possibly with effects on pigmentation; a laboratory study examined the mechanism of bimatoprost-induced eyelash growth [2][16]. Wikipedia also notes that the drug and its endogenous analogue have anti-adipogenic effects in laboratory work [1].

Bimatoprost is well absorbed through the cornea and starts lowering eye pressure around four hours after application, lasting at least 24 hours. Little reaches the bloodstream, with peak plasma levels at about 10 minutes and levels falling below detection by about 1.5 hours. Plasma protein binding is about 88 percent and half-life after intravenous infusion about 45 minutes [1].

Allergan developed bimatoprost as an antiglaucoma agent, and the US approved it for that indication in 2001 [1][2]. Increased lash growth was noted as a side effect in glaucoma patients, which led to development for hypotrichosis and FDA approval of Latisse in December 2008 [2]. Generic ophthalmic versions became available in 2015, and a sustained-release implant was approved in 2020, according to Grokipedia [2]. Wikipedia reports more than 1 million US prescriptions in 2023 [1].

A 2024 review states that US law does not require efficacy or safety assessment of over-the-counter eyelash serums before sale, and that some products contain prostaglandin analogues [8]. Latisse is the only FDA-approved drug for increasing lash length, thickness and darkness, per Grokipedia [2].
Research directions include sustained-release implants and inserts for glaucoma [14][24][25][26], and investigational uses in hair loss and anti-adipogenic effects [1][17].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org bimatoprost, usually under the brand name Latisse, is discussed as an eyelash treatment, with threads on application, side effects, eye colour change, import brands such as Careprost, and fat loss around the eyes [27][28][29][30].

claims.claim: Latisse grows longer, curlier lashes with few side effects.
Latisse can change eye colour, a concern for users with light eyes.
Bimatoprost reduces fat around the eye, which can reshape the eyelid.
Careprost is the same drug as Latisse.

timeline.event: FDA approves bimatoprost for glaucoma and ocular hypertension [1].
FDA approves Latisse for eyelash hypotrichosis [2].
Placebo-controlled eyebrow hypotrichosis study with Latisse begins [5].
